output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a multi-domain amnestic profile with severe impairment in episodic memory. Verbal learning and recall are markedly impaired (CVLT-3 long delay free recall z = -3.2; cued recall minimally better, reflecting a storage-type deficit). Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test 44/60), verbal fluency (FAS 27 words; animals 11/min), and executive function (Trail Making B 148 sec) are impaired. Visuoconstructive function is mildly impaired (Rey Complex Figure copy 24/36; delayed recall 6/36). Attention (Digit Span forward 5) is mildly reduced. Mood screen is within normal limits (GDS 4/15). Overall profile is consistent with amnestic mild dementia involving multiple cognitive domains

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 22/30 and MoCA 18/30 with an amnestic multi-domain profile and no cue benefit; brief staring pauses, an uncertain misperception, mild activated rigidity and no orthostatic drop documented; driving stopped and appointments supervised: mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: He has an amnestic decline with new spells and soft Lewy-type features, so the bedside assessment must record the profile, the fluctuation and parkinsonian signs and his function before any test is read [NIA_AA_2011] [DLB_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Multi-domain amnestic profile with severe storage-type memory impairment (minimal cue benefit), naming and fluency deficits, executive impairment; no purely visuospatial-predominant pattern; GDS within normal limits
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize the cognitive profile and establish baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Normed testing shows whether memory storage or attention and visuoperception lead the profile, which separates typical Alzheimer disease from Lewy body dementia, and sets a baseline [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No thyroid, renal, electrolyte or inflammatory cause; B12 248 pg/mL (low-normal on long-term metformin); glucose 128 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.1% from known diabetes; syphilis and HIV negative
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Treatable metabolic and endocrine contributors must be excluded before the decline is attributed to neurodegeneration [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid 0.52 umol/L, raised: mild functional B12 deficiency to treat
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to clarify the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A B12 of 248 pg/mL is indeterminate in a man on metformin for 9 years with reduced ankle vibration; methylmalonic acid shows whether there is tissue deficiency to treat [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral MTA grade 2 hippocampal atrophy with temporoparietal thinning; normal substantia nigra and basal ganglia without abnormal iron; no infarcts or mass
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a dementia volumetric protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and exclude structural causes
action_criteria.rationale: Hippocampal atrophy favours Alzheimer disease over Lewy body dementia, in which the medial temporal lobes are relatively preserved, and the MRI excludes vascular and structural causes [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive florbetapir PET (SUVr 1.47)
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal striatal dopamine transporter uptake bilaterally: no presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.label: Order DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) to test for a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.rationale: Staring spells, an uncertain misperception, activated rigidity and a brother with Parkinson disease raise Lewy body dementia, and reduced striatal uptake is an indicative biomarker for it [DLB_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two habitual staring spells captured without an ictal correlate; no epileptiform discharges
action_criteria.label: Obtain ambulatory video-EEG for the recurrent witnessed unresponsive spells, not as a routine Alzheimer diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Recurrent brief unresponsive spells in a man with Alzheimer-type decline can be focal seizures, which are more frequent in Alzheimer disease; capturing a habitual event answers the question [NICE_NG217].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose dementia with Lewy bodies from soft features alone (brief staring pauses, two uncertain visual misperceptions, mild activated rigidity) when the striatal dopamine transporter scan is normal and the profile, MRI and amyloid status point to Alzheimer disease

Do not start an antipsychotic for the visual misperceptions; they are uncertain and not distressing, and severe antipsychotic sensitivity occurs in Lewy body disease, which a normal DaTscan does not fully exclude
Do not start an antiseizure medicine for the staring spells after the ambulatory EEG captured them without an ictal correlate
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; memantine is for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Ask his wife at each visit about the Lewy body core features (fluctuating alertness, recurrent well-formed hallucinations, dream enactment, parkinsonism) and revisit the diagnosis if they become established [DLB_2017]
Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse (71 bpm), conduction history and current medicines [NICE_NG97].

Start vitamin B12 replacement for the raised methylmalonic acid on long-term metformin (for example oral cyanocobalamin 1000 micrograms daily, or intramuscular hydroxocobalamin per local practice) and continue metformin; B12 deficiency is a treatable contributor, not an alternative to the Alzheimer diagnosis [BSH_B12_2014].

Manage vascular risk to the targets for an older adult with mild dementia: HbA1c below about 8.0% (7.1% now) without hypoglycaemia, blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg (142/84 today, recheck), statin continued [ADA_older_adults_2026].

Explain that the ambulatory EEG captured his usual spells without seizure activity, so no antiseizure medicine is needed now, and re-investigate if the spells change (automatisms, longer events, falls or incontinence) [NICE_NG217].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Assess safety: he has stopped driving; review medication supervision, finances, kitchen and garden tool safety, hearing aid use and support for his wife
Disclose the diagnosis to him and his wife, discuss prognosis, and begin advance care planning (durable power of attorney, wishes for care) while he can take part

avoided_actions.rationale: The spells are brief staring pauses without loss of posture, and the ambulatory EEG showed sinus rhythm through both; pulse 71 and regular, no QT-prolonging medicine
No murmur, heart failure or embolic event; an echocardiogram does not answer the cognitive question
The spells were captured with sinus rhythm on the EEG's ECG channel, there is no syncope or palpitation, and standing blood pressure does not fall
MRI is possible and answers the atrophy and structural questions better than CT
MR spectroscopy is a research technique that does not change the diagnosis or management here

differential.key_features: Soft features raised it (staring pauses, two uncertain misperceptions, activated rigidity, a brother with Parkinson disease), but no core feature is established, the DaTscan is normal, memory storage leads the profile and the hippocampi are atrophic; Lewy co-pathology cannot be excluded

differential.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy (late-onset, including epilepsy associated with Alzheimer disease)
differential.key_features: Recurrent brief unresponsive spells raised it, but two habitual spells were captured on ambulatory video-EEG without an ictal correlate and there are no epileptiform discharges
Hypertension, diabetes and former smoking are risk factors, but white matter change is Fazekas 1 with no infarcts or microbleeds, insufficient for the degree of amnestic impairment

B12 248 pg/mL with raised methylmalonic acid is a mild functional deficiency and a treatable contributor; it cannot explain an 18-month storage-type amnestic decline with hippocampal atrophy and amyloid positivity
No early personality change, disinhibition or hyperorality; memory leads from onset and the atrophy is medial temporal and temporoparietal, not frontal
He is more withdrawn but denies low mood, GDS 4/15, and the storage-type deficit is not depressive
No parkinsonian motor syndrome (no bradykinesia or rest tremor), normal DaTscan, and the cognitive decline came first

key_clinical_evidence: Soft Lewy-type features (staring pauses, two uncertain misperceptions, activated rigidity, a brother with Parkinson disease) justify a DaTscan; a normal scan lowers the probability of dementia with Lewy bodies but does not diagnose Alzheimer disease [DLB_2017]
A storage-type amnestic deficit with bilateral hippocampal atrophy (MTA 2) and temporoparietal thinning, with amyloid positivity, is the signature of typical Alzheimer disease
Seizures are more frequent in Alzheimer disease, so recurrent unresponsive spells deserve an attempt to capture one; habitual events without an ictal correlate make epilepsy unlikely [NICE_NG217]
A low-normal B12 on long-term metformin with raised methylmalonic acid is a mild functional deficiency to treat, a contributor rather than the cause of the dementia [BSH_B12_2014]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Activated rigidity without bradykinesia, rest tremor or a parkinsonian motor syndrome is not the parkinsonism core feature of DLB; the DaTscan shows no presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
red_herrings.data_point: Mild bilateral upper-extremity cogwheel rigidity on activation and an older brother with Parkinson's disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward DLB or Parkinson's disease dementia; prompt a diagnosis of DLB on soft motor features alone

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Brief attentional pauses occur in Alzheimer disease and the ambulatory EEG shows no seizures; two uncertain misperceptions do not meet the DLB core feature of recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations; DaTscan is normal and amyloid status is positive
red_herrings.data_point: Brief blank-staring spells and two uncertain visual misperceptions (a small animal at home, a shadow in the examination room)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the staring spells as DLB-type fluctuation or as seizures, and the misperceptions as recurrent formed hallucinations, leading to a DLB or epilepsy diagnosis
red_herrings.location: History present illness and additional neurological exam

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: B12 248 pg/mL is within the reference range; methylmalonic acid shows a mild functional deficiency on metformin that should be treated, but it cannot explain a progressive multi-domain amnestic dementia with hippocampal atrophy and amyloid positivity
red_herrings.data_point: Vitamin B12 248 pg/mL at the low-normal end of reference range
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the amnestic decline to functional B12 deficiency and defer neurodegenerative workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude a mass lesion or hydrocephalus
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

findings.result: MMSE 22/30: lost 2 on orientation (date, month), 2 on serial sevens, 2 on recall, 1 on the three-stage command and 1 on figure copy.
MoCA 18/30: delayed recall 0/5 with no recovery from category or multiple-choice cues; naming 2/3; clock 2/3 (hands at 8:10 for 11:10); abstraction 0/2; serial sevens 2/3; orientation 4/6.

Two 5 to 10 second staring pauses during the interview with full resumption; he is unsure whether he saw a shadow behind the door. No sustained drowsiness, daytime sleep or disorganised speech between pauses.
Mild activated cogwheel rigidity in both arms, left more than right; no rest tremor or bradykinesia. Blood pressure 142/84 mmHg lying and 138/82 mmHg after 3 minutes standing, no symptoms.

Wife: 18 months of forgetting recent conversations and where things are stored, repeated questions within the hour, word-finding pauses; staring spells several times a week for 2 to 3 months; two uncertain visual misperceptions; no dream enactment, falls or incontinence; personality unchanged.
Stopped driving one month ago at his wife's request after getting lost on a familiar route; she now supervises his appointments. Independent in bathing, dressing and grooming.

clinical_assessment.impression: MMSE 22/30 and MoCA 18/30, with impairment in memory, orientation, naming, attention and executive function. Delayed recall 0/5 with no recovery from cues. His wife reports decline over 18 months, with brief staring spells and two uncertain visual misperceptions in the last 3 months. No parkinsonism beyond mild activated rigidity, and no orthostatic drop. He has stopped driving and his wife now supervises his appointments, so instrumental independence is lost: the syndrome is a mild dementia.

metadata.clinical_notes: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Recommended: MMA for a low-normal B12 on metformin. Optional: amyloid status by CSF or amyloid PET, DaTscan for the DLB differential, ambulatory EEG for witnessed unresponsive spells.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Recommended: MMA for a low-normal B12 on metformin. Optional: amyloid status by CSF or amyloid PET, DaTscan for the DLB differential, ambulatory EEG for witnessed unresponsive spells.
key_educational_points: Soft Lewy-type features justify a DaTscan; a normal scan argues against DLB but does not diagnose Alzheimer disease
Amyloid status can be shown by CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or by amyloid PET; one conclusive test is enough
Recurrent unresponsive spells in Alzheimer disease deserve capture on ambulatory EEG before any antiseizure treatment
metadata.real_seed_note: A systematic PMC search for a published CC-BY open-access case report of confirmed AD with DLB differential and normal DaTscan did not yield a verified, unambiguously CC-BY case meeting all criteria (72-year-old male, amnestic AD, normal DaTscan excluding DLB). This case was therefore authored as an authentic, clinically representative AD-vs-DLB puzzle consistent with published diagnostic criteria (NIA-AA 2011/2018, DLB Consortium 2017 McKeith et al. Neurology) without a specific PMID seed. The scenario is grounded in real-world clinical patterns documented in the DaTscan AD/DLB literature.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent 2026-08-10 recheck of Reviewer 1: case actions, authored reports and SFT pathway aligned; CSF and amyloid PET made non-duplicative alternatives
teaching_points: DaTscan is indicated when DLB is a genuine clinical consideration; soft features suffice to justify the test
A normal DaTscan is a strong argument against DLB but does not itself diagnose AD
Uncertain visual misperceptions and brief attentional pauses do not fulfil the DLB core diagnostic criteria
Activated cogwheel rigidity without a parkinsonian motor syndrome and with a normal DaTscan is insufficient for DLB

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Gerald Hoffman is a 72-year-old right-handed retired principal who presents to the neurology memory clinic accompanied by his wife, Eleanor, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past 18 months. His wife first noticed the changes approximately 18 months ago when he began forgetting recent conversations and misplacing items with increasing frequency — he would put keys in the refrigerator and forget where he had stored gardening tools he had used the day before. His longtime interest in crossword puzzles, which he previously completed in ink, has become notably more labored, and he now leaves many incomplete. Over the subsequent year his word-finding difficulties worsened: he frequently struggles to retrieve proper names and low-frequency nouns, sometimes describing rather than naming objects. His wife notes he has become repetitive, asking the same question within an hour.

In the past 2-3 months, new symptoms emerged that concern his wife: she has observed several episodes of blank staring lasting 5-10 seconds during which he does not respond, then resumes activity without any memory of the pause. These occur several times per week. He has also twice reported seeing something that was not there — once a small animal in the kitchen, and once a shadow in the examination room today. He has been somewhat more withdrawn and less interested in social activities, which Eleanor attributes to frustration with his memory. He denies feeling depressed. Sleep is adequate with good CPAP adherence; wife has not observed acting-out of dreams or nocturnal vocalizations. He remains independent in basic ADLs including bathing, dressing, and grooming. He stopped driving one month ago at Eleanor's request after he missed a turn on a familiar route and drove in the wrong direction for several minutes.

The family history is notable for an older brother with diagnosed Parkinson's disease, which Eleanor has read about and wonders whether her husband might have something similar. On careful questioning, she confirms that his personality is unchanged, there has been no new urinary urgency or incontinence, and no falls. He has not had obvious tremor at rest.

neurological_exam.additional: On two occasions during the interview, the patient appeared momentarily confused and stared blankly for 5-10 seconds, then resumed conversation without acknowledgment. Wife describes similar episodes at home, occurring several times per week over the past 2 months, which she attributes to him 'zoning out.' No incontinence, falls, or acting out of dreams reported. During history-taking, patient stated he 'saw a shadow move behind the door' in the examination room — when asked, he said he was not sure whether he truly saw something. Wife confirms one prior episode at home approximately 6 weeks ago where he said he saw a small animal in the kitchen; none has been verified.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow bilaterally. No dysmetria.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Face symmetric. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Hearing reduced bilaterally consistent with known hearing aid use. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Smell not formally tested.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait with slightly reduced stride length; mild stooped posture. Tandem gait mildly unsteady (1 step off at 6 steps). Romberg negative. No retropulsion on pull test. No en-bloc turning.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Oriented to person, place, and year but misidentifies the date as 3 days earlier and the month as one prior. MMSE 22/30: loses points on orientation (2), serial sevens (2), delayed recall (2), the three-stage command (1) and figure copy (1). MoCA 18/30: delayed recall 0/5 with no benefit from categorical cues, naming 2/3 (missed 'rhinoceros'), clock 2/3 (numbers correctly placed, hands set to 8:10 instead of 11:10), abstraction 0/2, serial sevens 2/3 and orientation 4/6. Attention and vigilance mildly reduced. Spontaneous speech is fluent with occasional word-finding pauses. Digit span forward 5 (mildly reduced), backward 3. Carries out a three-step command with one omission.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal. Tone normal at rest; mild bilateral upper-extremity cogwheel rigidity, more pronounced on the left, appears only with a contralateral activation maneuver. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No rest tremor. No bradykinesia or decrement on finger tapping. No postural tremor with outstretched arms.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis. 1+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Glabellar tap: 2 blinks then habituates. No grasp or palmomental reflex.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact in all extremities. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Mild vibratory reduction at bilateral ankles, attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
